title: MediaLit vs S3, UploadThing, Cloudinary & More
description: Compare MediaLit with Amazon S3, UploadThing, Cloudinary, Filestack, Vercel Blob and Supabase Storage: pricing, file limits, code and AI-agent access.

settings.content:
Compare

MediaLit vs the Alternatives

Picking a file upload service means comparing pricing pages, limits and quickstarts that never line up. We did that work for six popular options and put the results side by side: what you pay, how big a file can be, how much code it takes to upload a file and get a URL, and what you would have to build yourself. Where we could not confirm something, we say so.

MediaLit vs Amazon S3

S3 is the standard for object storage, and it does that job very well: 50 TB objects, bucket versioning and every AWS integration. What it leaves to you is the upload layer: IAM keys, bucket policies, CORS rules, presigned URLs, a database of what you stored, and CloudFront if you want a CDN. MediaLit is that layer, and when you self-host it can run on top of your own S3 buckets.

Questions

Is MediaLit built on S3?

MediaLit works with any S3-compatible storage. Self-hosted, you point it at your own AWS S3, Cloudflare R2 or MinIO buckets and keep the same API. The hosted service at medialit.cloud handles storage for you.

Does S3 charge for egress?

Yes. Data transfer from S3 to the internet is billed per GB after the first 100 GB a month (about $0.09/GB in the first tier). MediaLit's plans list unlimited uploads and downloads.

When is S3 the better choice?

When you need versioning, objects larger than 2 GB, or deep AWS integration, and you are happy to build presigned uploads, CORS and cleanup yourself.

MediaLit vs UploadThing

UploadThing is a polished upload service for TypeScript apps, with file routes and ready-made upload components. Both services start free and offer a $10/mo plan with 100 GB. The differences are in the details: MediaLit includes private files on its free plan, its server is open source and self-hostable, and agents can use it through a hosted MCP server and a CLI.

Questions

Which one is cheaper?

At small sizes they are close. UploadThing's free plan has 2 GB of storage and MediaLit's has 1 GB. Both have a $10/mo plan with 100 GB. MediaLit includes private files on the free plan; UploadThing adds them on paid plans.

Can I self-host either?

MediaLit, yes. The server is AGPL and runs on any S3-compatible storage. UploadThing's client libraries are open source, but the service itself is hosted only.

Can AI agents use them?

MediaLit has a hosted MCP server with OAuth, a CLI and an official Claude connector. At the time of writing, UploadThing has only a canary MCP package on npm.

MediaLit vs Cloudinary

Cloudinary is a full media platform: URL-based transformations, video streaming, AI tagging and a DAM. If you need on-the-fly image or video transforms, it does far more than MediaLit, which only makes thumbnails and optional WebP copies. If you need to store files and serve them, MediaLit is simpler and priced by storage instead of credits.

Questions

Does MediaLit transform images?

No. MediaLit makes thumbnails for images and videos on upload and can convert images to WebP. It has no URL-based transformations. If you need those, Cloudinary is the better fit.

How does Cloudinary pricing work?

In credits. One credit is 1 GB of storage, 1 GB of bandwidth or 1,000 transformations. The free plan has 25 credits a month; Plus has 225 for $89/mo billed yearly. MediaLit charges by plan: Pro is $10/mo for 100 GB.

Do both work with Claude?

Yes. Both have an MCP server and an official connector in Claude's directory.

MediaLit vs Filestack

Filestack pairs uploads with a file picker that pulls from 15+ cloud sources, plus transformations, document conversion and AI add-ons. Paid plans start at $69/mo. MediaLit focuses on storing and serving files, with a $10/mo Pro plan, a React uploader with resumable uploads, and an open-source server.

Questions

How do the prices compare?

Filestack's Start plan is $69/mo for 50 GB of storage, 75 GB of bandwidth and files up to 1 GB. MediaLit Pro is $10/mo for 100 GB and files up to 2 GB.

Does MediaLit have a file picker?

MediaLit has a drop-in React uploader that sends files straight from the browser over resumable uploads. It does not pull files from third-party sources the way Filestack's picker does.

What do the free plans include?

Filestack: 1 GB storage, 1 GB bandwidth, 500 uploads a month and 20 MB files. MediaLit: 1 GB storage and 50 MB files, with unlimited uploads and downloads listed.

MediaLit vs Vercel Blob

Vercel Blob is the natural pick inside a Vercel project: files up to 5 TB, Vercel's CDN, and since June 2026 private stores with signed URLs. It is billed by usage: storage, operations and data transfer. MediaLit is a flat plan that works the same from any host or framework, with a dashboard, temporary uploads that clean themselves up, and agent access over MCP.

Questions

Do I have to host on Vercel?

You need a Vercel account and a Blob store. Code running outside Vercel authenticates with a BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN. MediaLit works the same from any host, or you can self-host it.

How is Vercel Blob billed?

Hobby includes 1 GB of storage and 10 GB of transfer. On Pro, the $20/mo platform fee includes $20 of usage credit, then storage, operations and data transfer are billed per use. MediaLit Pro is a flat $10/mo for 100 GB.

Do both support private files?

Yes. Vercel Private Blob became generally available in June 2026, with signed URLs that last up to 7 days. MediaLit serves private files through signed URLs that expire, on every plan.

MediaLit vs Supabase Storage

Supabase Storage comes with a Postgres database, auth and row-level security, and like MediaLit it is open source and self-hostable. If you already run your app on Supabase, it is the obvious choice. MediaLit is storage only: no database project to manage, a drop-in React uploader, and temporary uploads that are deleted unless your app keeps them.

Questions

Is Supabase open source too?

Yes. Both can be self-hosted. Supabase self-hosts as a full backend with Docker; MediaLit needs PostgreSQL and two S3-compatible buckets.

What does each free plan include?

Supabase: 1 GB of file storage, 5 GB of egress and 50 MB files, and free projects pause after a week of inactivity. MediaLit: 1 GB of storage and 50 MB files.

Can AI agents use them?

Yes. Both have an MCP server, a CLI and an official connector in Claude's directory.
